title: British widow faces deportation from Sweden after 22 years
description: A 78-year-old British widow has told the BBC she is struggling to eat or sleep as the Swedish government threatens to deport her over a late post-Brex
body: A 78-year-old British widow has told the BBC she is struggling to eat or sleep as the Swedish government threatens to deport her over a late post-Brexit residence application.Joyce Thomas, a retired nurse, moved to Sweden 22 years ago with her husband, who passed away from cancer three years ago.The threat of deportation came after Swedish authorities said they should have made a formal application to stay in the country after Brexit.Thomas has since had numerous applications and appeals rejected, and Tuesday marks the latest deadline for her to leave voluntarily."This is absolute hell," she said from her home in Sweden."I can't sleep, I can't eat. You get up in the morning, you don't know what's going to happen."The Swedish migration minister told the BBC that the government would "examine whether there are measures we can take to make the process easier for those affected" by some consequences of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement.When the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020, British citizens stopped being EU citizens, which meant they could no longer stay in Sweden with right of residence status.During a transitional period, British citizens could apply for residence status under the withdrawal agreement between the UK and the EU - which ended on 31 December 2021.Thomas said she and her husband were unaware that they needed to submit an application and she was only informed of the rule once she attempted to re-enter the country in 2023.After years of appeals, the Migrationsverket, the Swedish government agency responsible for migration, told her last month that her voluntary departure deadline was 8 September.Her lawyers are arguing against the deportation, but she is still waiting to hear from the government.Thomas said the possibility of having to leave her son, grandchildren, friends and husband's grave has become too much to bear."I'm tired, I really am tired and I'm not young anymore," she said."Where is the empathy? I've lived here for more than 20 years - I've got friends, I've got family."According to Eurostat data, between 2021 and 2025, 2,490 UK nationals were ordered to leave Sweden. This is almost a third of more than 7,500 UK nationals ordered to leave the 27 EU Member States over this time period.The Migrationsverket said it could not comment on Thomas's case without her consent and did not respond to a question about how many British nationals are at risk of deportation. However, it told the Guardian last week that 458 British citizens had been deported or forcibly removed since Brexit.Last month, a family told the BBC how their father, who has dementia and vascular parkinsonism and is living in full-time care in Sweden, was also threatened with removal after more than two decades in the country.Swedish Minister for Migration, Johan Forssell, told the BBC that the current framework was implemented by a previous government and that it "will therefore look closely at the situation and examine whether there are measures we can take to make the process easier for those affected".He did not address Thomas's case directly but said "the government believes the rules should be applied generously"."The UK is a very important partner for Sweden, and we want British citizens who live and work in Sweden to be able to remain here," he said."We are currently in dialogue with the relevant Swedish authorities to get a clearer picture of what measures may be possible," he added.Håkan Svenneling, Thomas's MP from the opposition Vänsterpartiet (The Left Party), has criticised the government's "inhumane migration policy". "That is why I hope that Sunday's election in Sweden will be a turning point where the opposition can form a government and change migration policy so that Joyce and other Britons with strong ties to Sweden can stay here," he told the BBC.A spokesperson from the the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said: "We welcome the statement from the Swedish authorities that they will look at this issue. We are ready to support them in doing so."

schema.headline: British widow faces deportation from Sweden after 22 years

title: Paul Adams: British-Israeli relations at lowest ebb in decades
description: Israel's furious response to the British government's decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank testifies to just how i
body: Israel's furious response to the British government's decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank testifies to just how important this moment is.Britain took the brunt of Israel's anger, but the fact that 12 countries chose to move together clearly sharpened the sense of outrage.Officials in London always knew that such a dramatic shift in policy towards Israel-Palestine was going to elicit a hostile response, but seemed taken aback by the speed and ferocity of Israel's reaction.The closure of the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem, which serves the West Bank and deals directly with the Palestinian Authority in Ramallah, and the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Centre, the body set up last year to co-ordinate stabilisation and relief efforts in the Gaza Strip, are very hostile moves.They tell you that Israel is deeply troubled by Tuesday's action by the UK and 11 other countries, which include France, Spain and Canada.Products manufactured in settlements may not represent a significant proportion of Israel's exports, but the political symbolism of singling these out for special treatment is powerful.For decades, the British and other governments have regarded settlements in occupied Palestinian territory as illegal but stopped short of banning products grown or manufactured there.Now, having announced that Britain agrees with the 2024 International Court of Justice ruling that the occupation as a whole - including Israel's military presence - is unlawful, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband says the government's economic relationships must reflect that.Hence the ban, not just on products but also on companies that provide construction, infrastructure or finance to settlements. The measures, which also include restrictions on arms sales that "materially contribute to the occupation", go further than many expected.And it's not just the actions - it's the language of the foreign secretary's heartfelt, sometimes deeply personal statement that is so striking.As a "proud British Jew... unwavering in my support for the state of Israel," Miliband spoke more directly and starkly than practically any of his predecessors.That a British foreign secretary should say that "settler terrorism is rampant" and was responsible for the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians in parts of the West Bank, while the Israeli government "turned a blind eye to this" is truly remarkable.Miliband calls this a "reset" in British policy. At times today, it felt like a radical rethink, and it leaves British-Israeli relations at their lowest ebb for decades.Yes, the heated, febrile atmosphere that invariably accompanies an impending Israeli election may have contributed to Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar's brutal response, but most Israelis will have shared his sense of outrage.Many Israelis find the violent, messianic ideology of some settlers deeply problematic. Some see them as a national embarrassment. But that's not the same as saying they agree that settlements, built on land captured during the 1967 Six Day War, are illegal.Most would disagree violently with the former prime minister, Ehud Olmert, who last year accused his successor Benjamin Netanyahu of turning Israel into an international pariah.But they can feel the walls of international opprobrium closing in - from protests at Eurovision or sporting events, to international arrest warrants being issued against their leaders and now to bans on settlement products - and that makes them anxious and defensive.For the Palestinians, on the other hand, this feels like progress. The Palestinian foreign ministry commended the countries adopting sanctions but called for "urgent, concrete measures" to stop Israel's "illegal settlement enterprise".In London, the Palestinian ambassador Dr Husam Zomlot called the government's decision "a turning point in the UK-Palestine relationship".Britain's "courageous steps", he said, would help pave the way for the independence of the State of Palestine on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.But Zomlot knows that the reality of Israel's 59-year occupation has not ended, or even substantially changed.The prospects for a viable Palestinian state remain vanishingly small, and there's little immediate sign that concerted action by 12 countries will reverse Israel's seemingly inexorable takeover of the West Bank.Only the United States has that kind of influence, should it choose to wield it.In 1991, President George HW Bush and his steely Secretary of State James Baker threatened to withhold $10bn (£7.4bn) in loan guarantees from the government of Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir, when the famously tough Shamir refused to promise that it wouldn't be used to finance settlement activity in the occupied territories.But Donald Trump has so far shown no desire to curb Benjamin Netanyahu's settlement plans.Some parts of Trump's MAGA movement have turned against Israel in recent years, but the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, is a fervent Christian Zionist who shares Israel's view that the West Bank was promised to the Jews by God.So Tuesday's action by the UK and its partners pits them not just against Israel but also against Israel's backer-in-chief in Washington.

schema.headline: Paul Adams: British-Israeli relations at lowest ebb in decades

title: Monty Don to leave Gardeners' World after more than 20 years
description: Monty Don is to step down as the host of Gardeners' World after more than 20 years, the BBC has announced. The 71-year-old, who is the programme's lon
body: Monty Don is to step down as the host of Gardeners' World after more than 20 years, the BBC has announced. The 71-year-old, who is the programme's longest-serving head gardener, will leave at the end of the current series.In a statement, Don said working on the show had been a "deeply rewarding experience," but added: "Now is the right time for a change."The BBC said Don had "inspired and guided millions of viewers with his warmth, wisdom and passion for gardening" since joining the programme in 2003.Don began presenting the programme at Berryfields, a rented garden in Stratford-upon-Avon, before it moved in 2011 to his own garden, Longmeadow in Herefordshire. "Throughout that time - and around 700 programmes - I have had the privilege of sharing my own abiding passion for gardens and gardening with an equally passionate, and often equally knowledgeable audience," he said."That connection with millions, not just in Britain but across the world, who share a love of gardens, plants and the natural world is something I have always treasured and which I increasingly believe to be at the heart of a life well lived."Don added he had "always relished the craft of programme making" and paid tribute to the "superlative BBC team" he worked with over the years. "I look forward to continuing to work with and for the BBC on other projects, as well as following new avenues," he concluded. "And of course, I will still be gardening, dog by side, here at Longmeadow."The presenter, whose full name is George Montague Don, made his TV debut in 1989 with a gardening segment on ITV's This Morning.That led to further work on the BBC and Channel 4, a newspaper column, and the publication of more than 20 books about gardening authored by Don.He replaced Alan Titchmarsh on Gardeners' World in 2003, but took a break from the programme in 2008 as he recovered from a stroke.He has also presented other programmes including Around the World in 80 Gardens, My Dream Farm, Mastercrafts, Monty Don's Rhineland Gardens, and coverage of the Chelsea Flower Show.The BBC's chief content officer Kate Phillips described Don as "unique", adding he was "a wonderfully engaging broadcaster with a soothing, calm presence who has inspired so many"."Monty's decision to leave Gardeners' World is one I respect, but I'm still very sad he's leaving," she added."We are a nation full of budding gardeners, and his tips and advice have been invaluable to viewers for more than 20 years and have certainly helped me increase my knowledge as well as my plant survival rate!"I would like to thank Monty personally for his honesty and kindness which has seen him open up about his own personal struggles and the power of the natural world to improve mental health. We will miss him on the show hugely."Don has been open about his struggle with depression over the years.

schema.headline: Monty Don to leave Gardeners' World after more than 20 years

title: Glastonbury confirms ticket sale dates - and highest ever price
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, Olivia Rodrigo was the last act to perform on the Pyramid Stage in 2025, before Glastonbury took a fallow yearByMusic
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, Olivia Rodrigo was the last act to perform on the Pyramid Stage in 2025, before Glastonbury took a fallow yearByMusic correspondentUpdated 4 hours agoAfter taking a fallow year in 2026, the Glastonbury Festival has confirmed that tickets for next year's event will go on sale in October.Tickets for the weekend will cost £408 including a £5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of £29.50 from 2025.Headliners for the festival, which takes place from 23 to 27 June, have yet to be announced, but rumours are already swirling, with everyone from Harry Styles and Fontaines DC to Taylor Swift and Stevie Wonder said to be in the mix.Tickets for the festival typically sell out in less than an hour, with thousands of fans  joining online queues to fight for their place.In a post on the official Glastonbury Instagram page, external, organisers said tickets with coach travel would go on sale at 18:00 BST on Thursday, 1 October.General admission tickets go on sale a couple of days later, at 09:00 BST on Sunday 4 October.As part of an ongoing campaign to stop touts, anyone wanting to attend Glastonbury had to be registered in advance. You can check your registration on its website. , externalIn recent years, the festival has also introduced an automatic queuing system on the day of sale, with fans needing to be online before the start of the sale with a valid registration number.Festival prices rise across the boardGlastonbury, which features more than 100 stages, was already the UK's most expensive music festival, but next year's ticket prices are the highest ever - breaking the £400 barrier for the first time.The increase is part of a pattern across the industry.Analysis by BBC News found the cost of attending the UK's major festivals has surged over the past decade - rising above the rate of inflation.Parklife tickets have increased by around £69 (71%) in real terms since 2013 - while Reading and Leeds had a much smaller increase, rising by about £40 (14%) over the same period.In the same period, Glastonbury's ticket prices went up by about £85  - a 30% price hike.The price hikes have multiple causes - from increased energy and infrastructure costs to post-Brexit labour shortages. However, last weekend's Reading and Leeds festival held prices at their 2025 level, with passes costing £325, rising to £361 with early-bird entry.Glastonbury said they would not be commenting on today's announcement but, in 2023, Emily Eavis acknowledged it was a "challenging time" for festival organisers."We have tried very hard to minimise the increase in price on the ticket but we're facing enormous rises in the costs of running this vast show, whilst still recovering from the huge financial impact of two years without a festival because of Covid."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Madonna has hinted that she will perform in the UK next year, but has not said whereThe festival last took place in 2025, with Olivia Rodrigo, The 1975 and Neil Young topping the bill.Glastonbury organiser Emily Eavis recently scotched rumours that Madonna would be among the headliners for next year's event."No, it's definitely not Madonna, I'll tell you that," she told BBC Radio 4's PM programme."But we have got three [other] headliners and we're very excited about it - it's all coming together really well," she added.Asked about the possibility of a performance from Taylor Swift, Eavis laughed and said she didn't want to discuss the line-up any more.

schema.headline: Glastonbury confirms ticket sale dates - and highest ever price

title: Aston Villa: Champions League victory in Brugge gives Villa lift-off with first win of season
description: The visitors were in a commanding and deserved position at half-time, McGinn's opener making him the club's all-time record European goalscorer with 1
body: The visitors were in a commanding and deserved position at half-time, McGinn's opener making him the club's all-time record European goalscorer with 12. Buendia's strike and Jackson's first Villa goal - benefiting from Yann Sommer's rush of blood - had them cruising.Brugge were poor and George Hemmings, Villa's first Champions League/European Cup teenage starter in 43 years, could have had at least one. Yet the hosts made it uncomfortable for Emery's men with Nicolo Tresoldi's penalty after Aaron Wan-Bissaka's blatant handball setting up an anxious last half an hour, during which Tresoldi hit the post.It can be viewed as a blessing in disguise that Villa had to battle their way through and ride out the hosts' pressure to earn their first win of the season. Adding the grit and determination to the quality of the opening half to prove they can get the job done.Not that they needed the evidence themselves, Emery and his squad always have that faith and the internal desire to progress no matter the obstacle.It was the same last season. A below-par 1-0 win over limited Bologna - thanks to another McGinn goal - got Villa going and they hardly looked back.The victory kicked off the staggering run of 17 wins in 20 games which formed the backbone of returning to the Champions League and giving Villa momentum to win the Europa League.Since then, of course, Villa's spine has been torn out and Emery has to integrate 10 new players into his methodical methods. Three points in Brugge may not spark another relentless run but it gives Emery and Villa the foundations of this new era. "It's a new Villa and it was a big test for the new players to dig in," McGinn told Uefa. "It was Joao Gomes and George Hemmings' first Champions League game. It's not easy to go away at a place like this in difficult weather conditions. Club Brugge were pushing and pushing and pushing and we had to stand strong. We managed to do that."It was so important to show a real gritty performance and get a victory at a very, very tough place to play."After just one shot on target in their opening three Premier League games the nine Villa had in Belgium would have been a comfort to Emery.He said following Saturday's 0-0 draw at Hull it was vital to take the rebuild step-by-step and Tuesday's win was another positive move."The players have a responsibility too, the older players need to guide to keep our standard high, to show everybody that this is the only way to achieve our targets," Emery told the post-match news conference. "We are improving after Brighton and after Hull City."We must work hard - it is the only way. This is the process that we must try to set. We did one very important step forward, being resilient when we were struggling."His players wasted no time in making that next leap by having 14 attempts in the first half, with Hemmings going closest to adding more goals. Jackson, on his third start, got his first Villa goal following his record £65m move from Chelsea as he starts proving he is a fitting replacement for the departed Ollie Watkins. The striker, who worked with Emery at Villarreal, will be one of the flag-bearers of Villa's new beginning as both the record signing and the player expected to score the goals to ensure they can compete at the elite level again."We don't care about the past, we just focus on the next one. Like every team, we have our ambitions. We just know it's a long journey, so we take it step by step try to win every game we play," said the Senegal international. "I'm very happy to be here and happy to be with the team, manager and staff. Hopefully, there are many more to come."Villa now host Nottingham Forest in the Premier League on Saturday before going to Coventry in the Carabao Cup and then travelling to Tottenham.After returning from Belgium with three points following their stuttering start, they could go into the extended international break with a fresh perspective.

schema.headline: Aston Villa: Champions League victory in Brugge gives Villa lift-off with first win of season

title: More flight delays expected after hundreds cancelled by air traffic control glitch
description: Flight delays are expected to continue on Wednesday after an air traffic control problem cancelled hundreds of flights across the UK. Tens of thousand
body: Flight delays are expected to continue on Wednesday after an air traffic control problem cancelled hundreds of flights across the UK. Tens of thousands of passengers were affected by the disruption and tracking website FlightRadar24 said up to 1,000 flights were cancelled after a glitch affecting air traffic control provider Nats.Its boss Martin Rolfe apologised, telling the BBC there would be a full investigation into what had gone wrong, after Nats said resolving the issue had taken "longer than hoped".With few aircraft able to take off, it is understood landings were restricted, leading to some flights being unable to depart overseas airports.The fault was widespread across the UK, and beyond, with airports in Scotland and Ireland also reporting disruption. EasyJet made 200 cancellations and British Airways more than 100. It is not the first time disruption has blighted Nats' control system. Ryanair and Wizz Air called for an overhaul of the organisation, with Wizz Air saying Nats was "not fit for purpose" in its current form. When asked whether he was considering his position, Rolfe said there would be "lots of time for that later" but his focus now was on making sure the problem was solved.Europe's busiest airline, Ryanair, reported on Tuesday that more than 65,000 passengers had been delayed by up to eight hours.At Heathrow, one of the busiest airports in Europe, departures were initially paused around lunchtime. Traffic then resumed, before facing further disruption in the afternoon. It is understood the airport ran out of space for incoming flights during the afternoon because planes had not been departing. Thirteen Heathrow-bound flights were diverted to other airports in the UK and Europe.Passengers have been advised to contact their airlines to check the status of their flights.British Airways said in a statement that it was anticipating knock-on effects."We were forced to cancel or divert more than 100 flights on Tuesday afternoon," a spokesperson said."We're doing everything we can to keep our customers updated and make arrangements for them to continue their journeys."We ask customers whose flights have been cancelled not to travel to the airport and to bear with us if they're trying to get in touch, as our call centres are incredibly busy at the moment."Airports across the UK said they were experiencing cancellations and delays and advised people to check their flight details before travelling.According to FlightRadar, the worst affected airports were Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Birmingham. Ryanair said affected passengers would be notified.Phil White from Bexhill told BBC Your Voice that his flight to Lanzarote boarded on time but he was left sitting on the tarmac at Gatwick for hours."We've been told the radar is down and we can't take off," Phil said."It's comfortable enough but the pilots been on every 20 minutes saying they are waiting for information from air traffic control and when he finds anything out he will let us know."Even if Nats has resolved the issue with its flight processing system, the disruption is likely to persist due to backlogs.Rolfe said the issue was in Nats' flight data processing system. He said it was not the same system that failed during an incident in 2023 over the August Bank Holiday weekend.Although the technical issue affected departures, arrivals were also hit as space on the ground became increasingly restricted. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said that "it will take time to fully resume flights, so continue to check with airlines"."I am seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job," she wrote on X.According to Nats, the flight processing system processes flight plans and other operational information used by air traffic controllers to manage air traffic.The system continually updates flight information as aircraft progress through UK airspace, helping controllers maintain a safe and orderly flow of traffic.Chloe Davis,18, from Cambridgeshire was left sitting on a Virgin plane at Heathrow waiting to fly to Orlando.She told BBC Your Voice that she had been due to depart at 13:40 BST."I'm not concerned, I would just like to know what's going on," she said."There [are] planes parked up on the taxi way because there's no gates for them to go to."

schema.headline: More flight delays expected after hundreds cancelled by air traffic control glitch

title: Abuse of RNLI volunteers 'wholly unacceptable', chief says
description: In a statement issued on Tuesday, Sparkes said: "Recent events have generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding about the RNLI – our pu
body: In a statement issued on Tuesday, Sparkes said: "Recent events have generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding about the RNLI – our purpose, our tasking, and particularly our lifesaving work in the Channel."Sadly, as a result, some of our volunteers and staff have been the subject of online and, in the worst cases, physical abuse."The RNLI's people represent the very best in our society, they selflessly give up their time to keep others safe."He continued: "We will take whatever steps we can, to care for and protect our people and their families."Digital Secretary Lisa Nandy said she had spoken with tech firms about how the names, addresses and photographs of RNLI staff and volunteers were reportedly shared online.She was responding to Vikki Slade, the Liberal Democrat MP for Mid Dorset and North Poole, about "some very disturbing posts" on social media identifying "brave RNLI rescuers".Nandy was asked what more the government could do to remove posts "that put children and adults' safety at risk through doxxing".She told the Commons: "It is something that the government is concerned about [and] I'm personally concerned about."Requests to accept the landing of RNLI boats carrying the migrants were refused by both Portsmouth harbour and Southampton Port, the BBC understands.

schema.headline: Abuse of RNLI volunteers 'wholly unacceptable', chief says

title: The firms turning recruitment into X Factor-style competitions
description: Image source, Jon BradleyImage caption, Yumi Liberman, centre, and two friends pitched a business idea to French cosmetics company L'OrealByMaryLou Co
body: Image source, Jon BradleyImage caption, Yumi Liberman, centre, and two friends pitched a business idea to French cosmetics company L'OrealByMaryLou CostaUpdated 08:43 BSTYumi Liberman was up on stage in front of a panel of judges and an audience of 300 people, and she had to perform.But rather than singing, dancing or playing a musical instrument, she and two friends were in an auditorium in London in 2024 to pitch their business idea, hoping to secure a full-time job with cosmetics giant L'Oreal."It reminded me of when I used to do competitive sports growing up and the pressure would get heavy," says Liberman, now 24. "But somehow you just get into flow mode."She and her friends had got through to the UK final of Brandstorm, an international competition run by the French company, where young adults outline their product and business ideas.Their proposal for a haircare app saw them crowned UK winners and they went on to that year's global final in Paris where they came third.While only members of the team that finished first automatically got full-time jobs, Liberman had so impressed senior figures at the company that she managed to secure a place on its marketing management traineeship, with a full-time position at the end.Image source, Jon BradleyImage caption, Yumi Liberman is on track to get a full-time job with L'OrealTurning recruitment into X Factor-style competitions, with jobs as the prize, generates publicity and buzz for companies. But for the young people involved, is it exciting - or unfair?In the current global economic environment, youth unemployment is higher than the national average in many countries, as companies are reluctant to take on new staff. In the UK the unemployment rate for young adults is 16.2%,, external compared to the overall level of 4.9%., externalCompetitions like L'Oreal's can offer hope. But the vast majority of the 380,000 people around the world who applied for it this year, up 58% from 240,000 in 2025, didn't win anything.L'Oreal told the BBC that its Brandstorm competition works well because it helps the company attract a wider range of potential new recruits, including young people who wouldn't necessarily have thought of applying for a job at the firm.Yet while Liberman says she enjoyed the formal competition structure, others who have been through similar recruitment competitions are critical.'Intimidating'Melissa Alcruz now works in marketing for a US real estate business based in New York City, but in the past she did the same job for TV channel MTV.While at MTV she competed in an internal competition for a promotion that she says was referred to as a "bake-off". Candidates had to come up with sponsorship and marketing campaigns, and then pitch to a room of seven people."This is intimidating, even for a seasoned professional. I ultimately got the job, but even though I won I disliked the process," says Alcruz.She points out that she already had a demanding full-time role at the company, and was then "expected to complete several substantial projects" for the competition in her spare time.MTV's current parent company, Paramount Skydance Corporation, has been asked for a comment.Former recruitment consultant Katrina Collier, now an author, speaker and recruiter trainer, is concerned that competition-based recruitment processes that potentially require candidates to give up lots of their time for free can create "economic discrimination"."Not everyone can take time, possibly months, to participate in the challenges for the chance to secure one of a limited number of roles," she says. "Does that mean only people from financially strong backgrounds proceed?"Is that leaving talented applicants who don't have the bank of mum or dad, for example, unable to take part?"Image source, Melissa AlcruzImage caption, Melissa Alcruz says that such competitions can require the candidates to have to do too much workJamie Kohn, senior director for talent acquisition at research firm Gartner, reasons that competition-based hiring formats are here to stay because employers find it easier to evaluate candidates than via the traditional interview method.But she agrees that organisations need to be cautious about how much they ask of the jobseekers. "And they should focus on providing feedback… so candidates build their capabilities even if they are not selected."For psychologist Amanda Potter, her concern is that recruiting via competition events tend to favour extroverts, and therefore put quieter personality types at a disadvantage."Does this approach encourage all types of people to apply, or would certain types of people avoid these assessment methods?" she says. "This could result in an organisation [ending up] full of ambitious, competitive people who want to win, possibly to the detriment of others."However, Liberman, who lives with severe dyslexia, argues that going through a typical recruitment process and related assessments would have been more challenging for her.It has also meant that she managed to avoid any time spent unemployed after finishing university. Instead, she has gone straight into her chosen field, something she can't say about all of her peers."I have a lot of friends coming from extremely reputable backgrounds, extremely educated people who have applied to over 1,000 jobs, and have been jobless."Get in touchHave you been involved in a recruitment competition? Share your experience.

schema.headline: The firms turning recruitment into X Factor-style competitions

title: Forget the Mediterranean diet, I'm eating only food from Shetland for a month
description: Image caption, Dr Alex Armitage is eating only food produced in Shetland during SeptemberByJohn JohnstonBBC Scotland NewsReporting fromLerwickUpdated
body: Image caption, Dr Alex Armitage is eating only food produced in Shetland during SeptemberByJohn JohnstonBBC Scotland NewsReporting fromLerwickUpdated 8 September 2026 10:02 BSTCould you survive a month eating only food produced in your local area? It would be difficult enough to do in a city, town or village on the mainland. Dr Alex Armitage is doing it in Shetland. As part of Shetland Food Month, the consultant paediatrician has set himself the challenge of surviving on just local produce for the month of September.He's already been out in his kayak to catch fish, he's been foraging for mushrooms and berries, and he's enjoyed vegetables from his neighbour's croft.Figure caption, Dr Alex Armitage is eating only food produced in Shetland during SeptemberArmitage, who is also a councillor with the Scottish Greens, said he grew up in London where he heard stories of his granny's childhood in Shetland. He was fascinated by how people could survive on the archipelago, more than 100 miles north of the Scottish mainland. Now the population relies on the regular deliveries of food transported by Northlink ferry from AberdeenBut Armitage is concerned that increasingly stormy seas could leave the islands cut off for extended periods - and the supermarket shelves empty. "If we had a week the ferry doesn't come to Shetland and Tesco runs out of food, what would happen if that happened for longer and we really had to survive by ourselves here," he said. "It got me thinking could people actually survive on Shetland produce? I thought I would live out that thought experiment."Image caption, A Shetland feast: Boiled tatties, onions, tomatoes and coriander with Shetland butter and wild mushroomsImage caption, Whipped cream from the Shetland Dairy, with local raspberries and honeyThe father-of-one said he liked to start the day with a big breakfast - egg, fish and vegetables "fired up" in Shetland butter. "This morning I made Eggs Florentine with some eggs people have donated," he added. "I've also got a big shipment of herring which is a wonderful and a very traditional Shetland fish to fry."Most of the produce has been donated to him, but he buys Shetland milk and cream from a local shop. He added: "I like to use the opportunity of the Shetland Food Month to look deeper behind some of the stories about our food in Shetland."I've been out foraging. I've got mushrooms from Burra. I've just picked up blackberries from one of the lanes in Lerwick and I've been out fishing as well - I have a kayak. "Shetland tatties are very plentiful and very available. Shetland tatties are my favourite source of carbohydrate without a shadow of a doubt. Getting other sources of carbohydrates is extremely difficult."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Armitage said he enjoyed local eggs for his breakfastImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Shetland's waters provide a plentiful bounty of fishBut of course there are some items that just can't be produced in the cool Shetland climate. Asked what he is missing the most during his month-long challenge, he said: "It's got to be caffeine.""Fortunately I've got over the caffeine withdrawals," he said. "They were really hard, about three days. It's not pleasant, you just have a constant headache all the time."This is the third year that Armitage has challenged himself to eat just Shetland produce for a month. He said it was a fun activity but it was also an important reminder of the fragility of food security in the islands.

schema.headline: Forget the Mediterranean diet, I'm eating only food from Shetland for a month

title: Liam Gallagher's tambourine grin and Charli XCX says bye to Brat - Music Photography Awards 2026 shortlist
description: Striking images of Oasis's reunion tour and Charli XCX bringing Brat to Glastonbury Festival are among the nominees at this year's Abbey Road Music Ph
body: Striking images of Oasis's reunion tour and Charli XCX bringing Brat to Glastonbury Festival are among the nominees at this year's Abbey Road Music Photography Awards.The awards, which this year considered works by more than 24,500 submissions from 42 different countries, released a shortlist of 40 finalists across eight categories on Tuesday.The likes of Kendrick Lamar, Fontaines DC, Tame Impala and Sombr also feature in the shots, while other images of stars including FKA Twigs have been selected - out of competition - for judges' awards.All of the finalist photographs will go on display in the LED tunnel at entertainment complex Outernet London from 8 to 14 September.These will include the five pieces picked out for consideration in the fan-voted music moment of the year award.Voting is available online via the official website, external, and in person at the exhibition.The winners will be announced at a ceremony at the London studios - made famous by the 1969 Beatles album of the same name - on 24 September.

title: US Open 2026 results: Aryna Sabalenka fights back against Linda Noskova to keep title defence alive
description: Aryna Sabalenka thought she had lost her US Open crown before leaving herself "speechless" as she battled back to beat Linda Noskova in three sets and
body: Aryna Sabalenka thought she had lost her US Open crown before leaving herself "speechless" as she battled back to beat Linda Noskova in three sets and advance to the semi-finals.Taken to a deciding set for the first time in this year's tournament, the two-time defending champion trailed 4-2 in the third set and later 2-0 in the tie-break before recovering to close out a 7-6 (7-1) 3-6 7-6 (10-7) win in a little under two and a half hours.It was the 28-year-old's 19th consecutive win at the tournament, having not tasted defeat since the 2023 final, while she becomes the first woman since Serena Williams in 2016 to reach six successive semi-finals at Flushing Meadows.Victory also sees her temporarily keep hold of her world number one ranking, though she will be overtaken at the top regardless of how she fares in the remainder the tournament if world number two Elena Rybakina beats Zheng Qinwen on Wednesday.Asked if she would be happy if she retained her US Open title but Rybakina replaced her at the head of the standings, Sabalenka said: "I'll be more than happy. Three-peat - sounds great."I'm just super happy that I put myself in the position where I have chance to go for the three-peat, even though I'm still far away from that."Sabalenka will next face either American third seed Jessica Pegula or her compatriot Emma Navarro, seeded 26th, as she bids to reach a fourth consecutive US Open final.The Belarusian has a history of letting her emotions get the better of her, most recently in her quarter-final defeat from a set up at the French Open.But as in her previous match against Taylor Townsend, when she had her serve broken four times and trailed 3-1 in the second set, Sabalenka showed impressive composure to emerge victorious against Wimbledon champion Noskova, suggesting she may have turned a corner."I'm speechless right now. I was pushing to the limit in this match, especially in the third set," said Sabalenka."I honestly thought that that's it, the match is over, but probably that's what helped me to feel loose and go after my shots. [I'm] super happy to get the win."Sabalenka began the match in cruise control, breaking in sixth seed Noskova's opening service game and racing into a 5-2 lead, before being broken as she served for the set.Although she dominated the subsequent tie-break, the double fault she hit in her last service game – one of four in the match – would prove a feature of her performance, as would her failure to convert break points.She wasted three early in the second set before conceding a break in the sixth game with a double fault at 30-40 as Noskova forced a decider.After hitting two more double faults to be broken for a third time, she looked down and out after Noskova held to love for a 4-2 lead, but won the next three games to turn the match around.She then won the tie-break - for a 10th successive time at the US Open, in a run dating back to 2021 - to complete her comeback, sealing the victory with a nerveless second-serve ace.This was only Sabalenka's second quarter-final victory since March, with the top seed unable to replicate her early season hard-court success – which included titles in Brisbane, Indian Wells and Miami – on the clay or grass.She suffered last-16 exits in Toronto and Cincinnati in the build-up to the US Open, but has rediscovered something approaching her best form at the tournament where she is yet to lose a quarter-final in six attempts."I have to say that knowing that physically my body can handle these matches again, I'm super happy with that," Sabalenka said. "And of course, these kind of tight matches give you so much confidence that you're back and you're ready to do anything it takes to get the win. So this match definitely gives me a boost of energy and motivation."For Noskova, this defeat, during which she hit more winners, fewer unforced errors, and saved seven of her nine break points, ends a run of 11 consecutive singles wins at Grand Slams.

title: LIV Golf: Players free to leave after competition files for bankruptcy protection
description: LIV Golf has filed for bankruptcy protection with at least $45m (£33m) owed to players, who will now have the option to leave.A Chapter 11 petition, w
body: LIV Golf has filed for bankruptcy protection with at least $45m (£33m) owed to players, who will now have the option to leave.A Chapter 11 petition, which LIV says is to "preserve the company's business" as it attempts to restructure after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding, was filed in the United States on Tuesday.The breakaway league says it has found a new investor in BC Partners, following the decision in April by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) to pull its funding.Documents in the petition outline money owed to LIV Golf's creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims. Two-time major winner Jon Rahm tops that list with an unsecured claim of $7.5m (£5.5m).Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7m - £4.2m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m - £4.1m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m - £3.5m) and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m - £2.5m) are also among the top 30 creditors, as well as Brooks Koepka, who left to rejoin the PGA Tour in January but has an unsecured claim of $1.7m (£1.25m).The total amount owed to the 14 current and former LIV players in the top 30 creditors is just over $45m (£33m).The court documents show LIV estimates its assets at $100m-$500m (£74m-£370m) and its liabilities at between $500m and $1bn (£370m-£739m).LIV Golf intends to commence its new majority player-owned league early next year and it is understood the Chapter 11 process allows it to start talking to players about their participation in LIV's future.BBC Sport understands there is no obligation on players to sign on to LIV 2.0, regardless of whether they had previously signed multi-year contracts with LIV Golf.Sources have said contracts under the previous iteration of LIV Golf will finish because of this court filing, with amounts owed to players and other creditors addressed through the court process.However, it remains unclear when players would then be able to enter discussions with other tours.Since LIV's controversial launch in 2021, more than $5bn (£3.7bn) has been spent by PIF, with major winners including Rahm and DeChambeau lured by lucrative contracts and vast prize money.However, the future of the concept - and its star players - has been shrouded in uncertainty, with the 2026 season having ended early.LIV Golf chief executive Scott O'Neil told the BBC at the final event in Indianapolis last month he had "high levels of confidence" in achieving a "critical mass" of players to make the new league a reality.DeChambeau said at the conclusion of that event he felt there was "a lot of potential moving forward" and he believed there was "something fun coming".Speaking on Tuesday before this week's Irish Open, Rahm was tight-lipped when pressed on his future.Asked if he knew what the coming months held, he told BBC Sport: "Yes and no. It hasn't really changed from my last interview in Indianapolis."There's just a lot of things in place, right? There's a lot of things that could happen and it's one of those things where time's gonna tell."Rahm added: "I still have a contract with LIV 1.0 that I'm more than willing to fulfil, so like I said, time will tell."The bankruptcy filing was made in the federal district court of New Jersey, where LIV Golf set up a subsidiary earlier in the summer.Chapter 11 protection postpones a US company's obligations to its creditors, giving it time to reorganise its debts or sell parts of the business.PIF is providing a bankruptcy loan of $49.6m (£36.6m) - called 'debtor in possession' (DIP) financing - to help fund the process.When announcing its decision to withdraw funding, PIF said the "substantial investment required by LIV Golf over a longer term" was "no longer consistent" with its strategy.Despite its decision to stop bankrolling LIV Golf, PIF added it "remains committed" to its "substantial current and future investments in various sports as a priority sector".On Tuesday, LIV confirmed international investment firm BC Partners as its proposed new investor in a letter to fans outlining its "next phase"."LIV Golf has entered a court-supervised restructuring process that provides us with the time and framework to address previous financial obligations and complete a transaction that will make the league's next phase a reality," said the letter."Put simply, this process is designed to build a stronger and more sustainable future for LIV Golf."O'Neil added in a statement: "This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf - one built around the fans, an innovative, player-first ownership model, and a part of the global golf ecosystem."In yet another indication the free-spending days of LIV 1.0 are over, the letter said the new league would be "built around a sustainable business model".Players are set to be given equity and individual commercial rights are set to be returned to players, giving them greater earning potential. In terms of prize money, LIV Golf purses are set to be lower than events on the PGA Tour - which has risen in part because of the existence of LIV - but higher than events on the DP World Tour.The letter also outlined proposed changes, with field sizes expanding to 75 players, the introduction of a cut, creating qualifiers and having more teams that "embrace national identities", with the ambitions for teams to "grow into enduring global sports businesses".

title: Renoir paintings worth millions stolen in French museum heist
description: Two paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been stolen from a museum in the south of France.Two thieves broke into the Renoi
body: Two paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been stolen from a museum in the south of France.Two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer early on Tuesday, seizing four paintings but dropping two of the works in the museum gardens as they escaped, local Mayor Bryan Masson said.The paintings, each worth €9m (£7.7m; $10.4m), are the latest high-profile pieces to have been stolen in a string of recent heists in Europe which have thrust the security of art in galleries and museums into the spotlight.One of the most high-profile was in October last year, when a brazen heist at the Louvre Museum in Paris saw France's priceless crown jewels being stolen.CCTV footage captured the thieves entering the Renoir museum gardens by cutting through a fence before they cut through structures holding the paintings' frames in place, the local mayor said.The alarm went off at 05:48 (03:48 GMT), and police were at the scene within five minutes, Masson explained, saying the thieves fled the scene upon hearing the security alarms.He later told reporters that the thieves seemed to be "well-equipped" and "well-informed".They were "wearing helmets, gloves, and combat gear" and carrying "an electric knife and hacksaw," he added.Investigators have found two zip-up bags at the scene, which may have belonged to the suspects.

schema.headline: Renoir paintings worth millions stolen in French museum heist

title: Iceland summons US ambassador over Trump's stars and stripes map
description: Iceland has summoned the US ambassador after President Donald Trump posted a map on social media that appeared to show Iceland and several other count
body: Iceland has summoned the US ambassador after President Donald Trump posted a map on social media that appeared to show Iceland and several other countries covered by the American flag. Trump posted the image on Truth Social on Monday, showing the US, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean covered in stars and stripes. The entire landmass was labelled "United States of America".Iceland's foreign minister said the post was "completely inappropriate".Trump's territorial ambitions have repeatedly strained relations with neighbouring countries, including his push to acquire Greenland and calls to make Canada the America's 51st state.His post of the map did not include a caption and preceded a  flurry of posts of maps renaming the US state of New Mexico as "New America". Responding to Trump's post, Iceland's Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir called in US ambassador to Iceland Billy Long, who formally took up the post last month, local media reported.When an ambassador is summoned, it typically means they are being called for a formal meeting, where the host country will express displeasure over their government's actions.The post also drew criticism from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who said on Monday that the position of Greenland's government and people had been made clear."The Greenlandic government and the Greenlandic people have said again and again that they do not want to be American," she told Danish news agency Ritzau in Nuuk. "I hope no one is in any doubt about that, either in the United States or the rest of the world."Trump's interest in Greenland has been a recurring theme on his social media accounts and in speeches since he took office again last year, claiming the island is necessary to the US to shore up its national security.His post came shortly after the European Commission announced a €200m (£172m) investment in the Danish territory during a visit by Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and Frederiksen. The European Commission said its investment would focus on education, internet connectivity, the use of raw materials in the country and hydropower energy.Meanwhile, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Mexico "is neither nor will be a colony or protectorate of any foreign country," after Trump's post.  "Proudly we are a free, independent, and sovereign nation," she wrote on social media.

schema.headline: Iceland summons US ambassador over Trump's stars and stripes map
